title: The Importance of Being Sincere
author: O. Alan Noble
source: You Are Not Your Own (Substack), November 28, 2025
summary: Prompted by a Twitter exchange in which one critic defended his character while disagreeing with his politics — granting that he 'came to his position honestly' — Noble makes a case for sincerity as a civic virtue in an era of reflexive suspicion. He names the underlying pathology as Bulverism, C.S. Lewis's term for dismissing an argument by impugning the arguer's motives rather than engaging the argument, and argues that a society that assumes everyone holds their views in bad faith loses the very possibility of persuasion and dialogue. He distinguishes this from naivety: there are genuine trolls and bad-faith actors, especially online, whom one can rightly disregard. But the discipline he commends is the 'act of hope' that a rhetorical opponent holds their beliefs sincerely and deserves a good-faith reply, paired with a duty to hold one's own beliefs sincerely — to be slow to speak, to seek purity of motive, and to avoid taking positions merely to be seen taking them. He warns that suspicion, now accelerated by AI-driven doubt about whether one's interlocutors are even human, could be 'the death of us as a culture,' and that the alternative to disagreement-with-understanding is a politics of brute force and will to power.
points: Noble diagnoses the cultural problem as Bulverism — Lewis's fallacy of attacking the arguer's motives instead of the argument — and argues an 'insincere society' where everyone is suspect forfeits the possibility of persuasion and dialogue.

He treats the charitable assumption as an 'act of hope': choosing to believe an opponent holds their views honestly, which builds the common ground that public discourse requires, without pretending genuine bad-faith trolls don't exist.

The virtue cuts both ways: sincerity obliges holding one's own beliefs tightly and honestly — being slow to speak until confident, and seeking purity of motive rather than posturing to be 'seen' caring.

He frames the stakes as civilizational: a society that can disagree while understanding one another can negotiate its challenges, while one that cannot has recourse only to 'brute force, will-to-power.'

He argues AI is accelerating the collapse of trust — when one can't tell whether half the trolls online are even human — so combating suspicion now requires the deliberate virtues of hope, prudence, and courage.
quotes: In an insincere society, everything and everyone is up for suspicion and scorn.
The ability to disagree affably is a supreme virtue, to disagree with your opponent precisely and carefully and even forcefully and yet gracefully.
We fall into this fallacy all the time in the contemporary world, a suspicion of our neighbor’s motives which distracts us from his or her arguments.
We should be able to say, “I think you are deeply wrong, but I understand how you came to your position.
Suspicion may be the death of us as a culture. And A.I. is only accelerating this problem.
A society of individuals who can disagree while understanding each other can negotiate and navigate challenges together, not perfectly, but possibly, with sacrifice.
